title: Tattoos speak of a young life indelibly marked by tragedy; Woman, 21, copes with grief of losing 3 loved ones by inking memorials to slain sister and boyfriend
article: Three times in three years has tragedy touched Nicole Fetterly.

Her younger sister was killed by an ex-boyfriend in 2007. Her uncle was killed by a Toronto police officer in 2008. Then last week, her live-in boyfriend was shot dead in their apartment, accidentally, while Fetterly listened to music in the neighbouring room.
At just 21 years old, hers is a life that has become about death. She dreams of going back to school, but it has been one thing after another.

"I ask myself every day 'How do I keep breathing?'" she says on a recent afternoon. "I don't really know how I feel about heaven or hell - sometimes I just get so mad - but I believe in somewhere. There has to be something. I just don't know why I keep losing the people who are the most close to me."
Fetterly has an appointment at Glass Head tattoo shop on Yonge St. She's a bit early, so she buys a pop at a pizza shop to kill time.
"When Chantele died, I had these angel wings done," she says pulling the neck of her pink top down. "For Bubz, I want to get something with hearts around it on the other side."

Bubz, as everyone called him, was Fetterly's boyfriend, 17-year-old Patrick John Smith. Toronto's 34th homicide of the year. It was the first Tuesday in August at around 10 30 p.m. Smith was hanging out in the living room with his best friend. Fetterly was listening to music in the bedroom.

"I had the music turned up, so I didn't really notice what it was at first, but there was this loud - pop!" she says. "I went out into the living room and Bubz was just slouched over on the couch moaning." The friend was in shock, she says. "He just kept saying 'Oh my god. Oh my god. I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry.'"
Fetterly screamed to call a cab.

"I kept thinking of the night Chantele was killed," she says. "The ambulance took like an hour. I thought it would be faster to just take a cab." The friend threw Smith over his shoulder and they headed to the front of her St. Lawrence Market area building. Within a few minutes, they were headed to St. Michael's Hospital.
He wasn't breathing.
"I'm pretty sure he died on the way," she says trailing off.
Quincy Callaghan-Thomas, 18, of Toronto, has been charged with manslaughter. Det. Doug Sansom says he believes Callaghan-Thomas' account and that, however careless, the shot was an accident.

"I just wish I had known. I can't believe there was a gun in my house," she says. "I didn't even know any of his friends carried guns ... I wish I had seen it and been like, 'What are you doing with that? Get out of here.'"
She speaks without emotion. She can hardly cry anymore.

Fetterly reaches for a black mesh basketball jersey that she has slung over her shoulder. She absent-mindedly brings it to her face and takes a deep breath. It was his favourite shirt and it still smells like him, she later explains.
She and Smith had been a couple for two years, but they had known each other since he was in diapers.

"At first we kept it a secret from everyone," says Fetterly, smiling for one of the few times that afternoon. "I'm older than him, (by nearly four years) and our families are close." She pauses and laughs, "I dropped him once when he was a baby."

Smith's mother, Kellie, says at first she was shocked to find out her son was dating the older Nicole. "But I'm glad it was her. She was a great influence on my son. I think one of the best in his life. God - I don't know how that girl is doing it right now. She's been through so much."

Fetterly's mother, Sandra Fetterly-Brown, is worried about her. "She's totally shut down on me. And we always had been really close and had good communication, with all we've been through," said the 40-year-old, who said no matter what her daughter says, she's taking her home for a few weeks to Hamilton.
Fetterly thought she and Smith would be together forever. He was the one she relied on for support through everything. They got together a month after Chantele was killed.

It was July 3, 2007. Chantele was living in Hamilton community housing with her mother, Fetterly-Brown, and younger brother. Chantele left their townhouse to go babysit a few doors down. On the way, she bumped into her ex-boyfriend, a troubled 16-year-old who the family had taken in at one point. Chantele owed him $10 and they started to argue.

According to the agreed statement of facts Chantele stormed inside and came back with a kitchen knife, pointing it in a "threatening manner." He yelled at her, then knocked her to the ground and walked away. Twice, she ran after him, and twice he knocked her down, then kicked her. He disappeared into a nearby unit and came back with another knife.
In a "sweeping circular motion" he thrust the blade into her chest, severing her aorta. She collapsed forward and he struck her on the head with the knife handle.

The Fetterlys launched an online petition to have the teen tried as an adult. Despite thousands of signatures, nothing came of it. Several dozen family and friends would gather with placards outside the courthouse, demanding officials try him as an adult. Smith was there through all of it.

In the end, the teen pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was given a little over three years in jail, including time served. His lawyer, Dean Paquette, would explain that "Based on the circumstances of the event, based on the fact he was 16, based on the fact she was using the knife in a threatening fashion ... 3.5 years in real jail is a significant penalty and significant consequence to his conduct."

For the Fetterlys it was a slap in the face. It comes down to money and status, she says. "Look at the Stefanie Rengel case," she says, referring to the recent court decision, which saw 17-year-old Melissa Todorovic convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced as an adult. "Don't get me wrong, I'm glad she's getting the time she deserves. But for us, she wasn't even there. She wasn't holding the knife. She was telling her boyfriend to do it and she's getting life in prison," says Fetterly. "(Rengel's) parents are cops. Where is our justice?"

It was also around this time, that Fetterly's uncle, David Fetterly, was killed. He had been in and out of jail much of his life, battling depression, bipolar disorder and addiction. But family is family. He was very close with Fetterly's mom and a great support during the trial.

In March 2008, the 42-year-old broke into a Roncesvalles pharmacy. A patrolling officer noticed the alarms going off and investigated. The province's Special Investigations Unit would later clear the officer of wrongdoing.
"The night I found out about Uncle Dave was the first time Bubz said 'I love you,'" says Fetterly.
It's 3:30 p.m. and the tattoo artist is free. He shows her a design of gothic lettering and blood red hearts. Her eyes brim with tears.
